Hatchlings of the Ornate dragon emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs after an incubation period lasting 111 days [ab = 111 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a developmental duration that reflects the relatively slow metabolic rate of this agamid species. At emergence, these neonates exhibit a mean snout-vent length of 3.565 cm [Lb = 3.565 cm], a measurement derived from twenty-three individuals incubated between 27 and 31 °C. Their corresponding wet weight at birth averages 1.844 g [Wwb = 1.844 g], based on a sample of twenty-four hatchlings from the same captive cohort. This modest body mass at hatching is consistent with an initial investment in yolk-dependent embryos that rely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. Comparative data from related agamids indicate that such a combination of extended incubation and small hatchling size is typical of species inhabiting semi-arid regions, where thermal variability during the nesting season may impose constraints on embryonic development.

During the early post-hatching period, juvenile Ctenophorus ornatus undergo a rapid phase of somatic growth as they transition from yolk-sac larvae to actively foraging young-of-year reptiles. Females achieve sexual maturity upon reaching a snout-vent length of 6.8 cm [Lp = 6.8 cm], a threshold corroborated by field observations of visible egg follicles reported by Baverstock in 1972 and supported by subsequent work by Lebas. At this size, the wet weight of pubertal females averages 12.97 g [Wwp = 12.97 g], a value derived from nine individuals captured in the field at the critical size boundary. First reproduction in females occurs at 316 days after hatching [tR = 316 days after hatching] when reared in the laboratory at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], based on the growth trajectories of seven individuals. This relatively early onset of reproductive capacity, achieved within the first year, suggests an adaptive strategy to maximize lifetime reproductive output in a seasonally arid environment.

Reproductive activity in female Ornate dragons is markedly influenced by thermal conditions, with maximum fecundity occurring during the warmer months. Wild females produce up to three clutches per breeding season, with each clutch containing up to four eggs as determined by palpation [N_R_i = each clutch containing up to four eggs as determined by palpation]. The corresponding frequency of reproductive events is approximately 3 clutches per season [F_R_i = approximately 3 clutches per season], a rate that peaks when ambient temperatures average 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C] during the active season. The eggs themselves have a mean wet weight of 1.595 g [Ww0 = 1.595 g], based on a sample of thirty-three eggs laid in captivity by wild-caught females. This moderate egg mass, combined with the capacity for multiple clutches, indicates a reproductive strategy that balances per-offspring investment against the potential for high annual fecundity, a pattern commonly observed in agamid lizards from unpredictable environments.

Adult body size in Ctenophorus ornatus shows clear sexual dimorphism, with males attaining considerably larger dimensions than females. The largest male ever captured during extensive field surveys encompassing approximately two thousand individuals reached an ultimate snout-vent length of 10.91 cm [Li = 10.91 cm]. The corresponding maximum wet weight recorded for adult males is 39.15 g [Wwi = 39.15 g], representing the extreme upper end of the size distribution for this species. This substantial adult body mass is notable among Australian agamids and likely confers advantages in male-male competition for territories and access to receptive females. The growth trajectory leading to these extreme sizes involves sustained feeding activity and efficient thermoregulation, as larger individuals must balance the energetic costs of maintenance against the benefits of increased dominance.

Longevity in the wild is modulated by both intrinsic physiological constraints and extrinsic ecological pressures, with the oldest documented individual reaching a lifespan of 2500 days [am = 2500 days] when maintained at 25.3 °C [T = 25.3 °C] under semi-natural conditions. This maximum recorded longevity of nearly seven years is relatively high for a small-bodied agamid and may reflect the species' occupancy of granite outcrops that provide both thermal refugia and protection from predators.
